claim: TGN46 is a transmembrane protein that functions as a receptor for the export of secretory cargo protein PAUF in CARTS.
source: Here, we identified the human transmembrane protein TGN46 as a receptor for the export of secretory cargo protein PAUF in CARTS – a class of protein kinase D-dependent TGN-to-plasma membrane carriers.
evidence: The abstract directly states this finding as a main result of the study.

claim: TGN46 is necessary for cargo sorting and loading into nascent carriers at the TGN.
source: We show that TGN46 is necessary for cargo sorting and loading into nascent carriers at the TGN.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this as a demonstrated finding.

claim: The lumenal domain of TGN46 encodes for its cargo sorting function.
source: By combining quantitative fluorescence microscopy and mutagenesis approaches, we further discovered that the lumenal domain of TGN46 encodes for its cargo sorting function.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this discovery based on experimental approaches.

claim: PAUF-MycHis secretion is reduced by approximately 75% in TGN46-KO cells compared to control cells.
source: In TGN46-KO cells, PAUF-MycHis secretion was reduced by ~75% as compared to control cells (Figure 1A).
evidence: The text states a specific quantitative reduction in secretion, supported by data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: A lower molecular weight form of PAUF-MycHis appears in the lysate of TGN46-KO cells, suggesting incomplete processing.
source: We noticed the appearance of a lower molecular weight form of PAUF-MycHis in the lysate of TGN46-KO cells (Figure 1A), suggesting that the processing (e.g., glycosylation) of intracellularly accumulated PAUF-MycHis is incomplete, and opening the possibility of a role for TGN46 in facilitating cargo glycosylation.
evidence: The observation is stated in the text and supported by Western blot data in Figure 1A.

claim: PAUF-mRFP efficiently exits the ER in the absence of TGN46.
source: Immunofluorescence microscopy of cells expressing PAUF-mRFP (monomeric red fluorescent protein) revealed its presence in a perinuclear compartment in both parental and TGN46-KO cell lines, indicating that PAUF-mRFP efficiently exits the ER in the absence of TGN46 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The text interprets microscopy data showing perinuclear localization in both cell types.

claim: The number density of PAUF-mRFP-positive punctate structures (CARTS) is significantly reduced by approximately 50% in TGN46-KO cells compared to parental cells.
source: Our data show that the number density of PAUF-mRFP-positive punctate structures – which define CARTS (Wakana et al., 2012) – is significantly reduced by ~50% in TGN46-KO cells as compared to parental cells (Figure 1B).
evidence: The text provides a specific quantitative measurement supported by data in Figure 1B.

claim: The number density of VSVG-containing carriers is unaltered upon TGN46 depletion.
source: In contrast, the number density of VSVG-containing carriers was unaltered upon TGN46 depletion (Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B), indicating that TGN46 selectively functions in the export of a subset of cargo proteins at the TGN.
evidence: The text states this observation and provides supporting microscopy data.

claim: TGN46 selectively functions in the export of a subset of cargo proteins at the TGN.
source: In contrast, the number density of VSVG-containing carriers was unaltered upon TGN46 depletion (Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B), indicating that TGN46 selectively functions in the export of a subset of cargo proteins at the TGN.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the differential effects on PAUF vs VSVG carriers.

claim: TGN46 depletion does not increase the proportion of CARTS that also contain VSVG.
source: In addition, TGN46 depletion did not increase the proportion of CARTS (defined as carriers positive for PAUF) that also contained VSVG (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The text states this observation with reference to supporting data.

claim: In the absence of TGN46, PAUF is not re-routed toward alternative TGN export routes such as VSVG-containing transport carriers.
source: These data strongly suggest that, in the absence of TGN46, PAUF is not re-routed toward alternative TGN export routes (particularly to that of VSV-G-containing transport carriers), and therefore bona fide CARTS are still formed, although at a strongly reduced rate.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the colocalization data.

claim: Bona fide CARTS are still formed in the absence of TGN46, although at a strongly reduced rate.
source: These data strongly suggest that, in the absence of TGN46, PAUF is not re-routed toward alternative TGN export routes (particularly to that of VSV-G-containing transport carriers), and therefore bona fide CARTS are still formed, although at a strongly reduced rate.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the experimental observations.

claim: PAUF-mRFP has a longer Golgi residence time in TGN46-KO cells (approximately 40 min) compared to control cells (approximately 25 min).
source: Our FLIP results showed that PAUF-mRFP has a longer Golgi residence time in TGN46-KO cells (~40 min) as compared to control cells (~25 min), and therefore TGN46 is necessary for an efficient and fast export of PAUF (Figure 1C, D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The text provides specific quantitative measurements from FLIP experiments.

claim: TGN46 is necessary for an efficient and fast export of PAUF.
source: Our FLIP results showed that PAUF-mRFP has a longer Golgi residence time in TGN46-KO cells (~40 min) as compared to control cells (~25 min), and therefore TGN46 is necessary for an efficient and fast export of PAUF (Figure 1C, D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the FLIP experiments.

claim: TGN46 is necessary for CARTS-mediated PAUF export from the TGN.
source: Taken together, our results indicate that TGN46 is necessary for CARTS-mediated PAUF export from the TGN.
evidence: This is stated as a summary conclusion from multiple experiments.

claim: Expression of kinase-dead mutant of PKD (PKD-KD) leads to the formation of cargo-loaded tubules at the TGN.
source: Cargo-loaded CARTS detach from the TGN once the neck of the nascent carrier is severed through a membrane fission reaction, a process regulated by the kinase activity of PKD (Wakana et al., 2012). Accordingly, expression of a kinase-dead mutant of PKD (PKD-KD) leads to the formation of cargo-loaded tubules (fission-defective CARTS precursors) at the TGN (Malhotra and Campelo, 2011; Wakana and Campelo, 2021).
evidence: This is stated as an established observation with citations to prior work.

claim: TGN46 depletion does not affect the number or appearance of PKD2-KD-Flag-positive TGN tubules per cell.
source: We first observed that TGN46 depletion did not affect the number or appearance of PKD2-KD-Flag-positive TGN tubules per cell (Figure 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 1E), suggesting that TGN46 is not necessary for membrane bending.
evidence: The text states this observation with reference to supporting microscopy data.

claim: TGN46 is not necessary for membrane bending.
source: We first observed that TGN46 depletion did not affect the number or appearance of PKD2-KD-Flag-positive TGN tubules per cell (Figure 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 1E), suggesting that TGN46 is not necessary for membrane bending.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the tubule formation data.

claim: In control (TGN46-positive) cells, a large fraction of Golgi tubules (approximately 75 ± 15%) contain both TGN46 and PAUF-mRFP.
source: Next, we observed that in control (TGN46-positive) cells, a large fraction of Golgi tubules contained both TGN46 and PAUF-mRFP (~75 ± 15% of tubules containing PAUF) (Figure 1E), as previously described (Liljedahl et al., 2001; Wakana et al., 2012).
evidence: The text provides a specific quantitative measurement with reference to supporting data and prior literature.

claim: PAUF-mRFP is absent from the majority of tubules induced by PKD2-KD-Flag in TGN46-depleted cells (approximately 45 ± 10% of tubules containing PAUF).
source: In contrast, and remarkably, PAUF-mRFP was absent from the majority of the tubules induced by PKD2-KD-Flag in TGN46-depleted cells (~45 ± 10% of tubules containing PAUF) (Figure 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: The text provides a specific quantitative measurement with reference to supporting data.

claim: TGN46 is required for sorting and loading the secretory cargo protein PAUF into nascent CARTS at the TGN.
source: These findings strongly indicate that TGN46 is required for sorting and loading the secretory cargo protein PAUF into nascent CARTS at the TGN.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the PKD-KD tubule experiments.

claim: TGN46 is a single-pass type-I transmembrane protein of 437 amino acids.
source: As TGN46 is a single-pass type-I TM protein of 437 amino acids (human TGN46, UniProt identifier O43493-2), we investigated whether functional cargo-packaging modules can be found in (1) the N-terminal lumenal domain (amino acids 22–381), (2) the single TM domain (TMD; amino acids 382–402), and/or (3) the short C-terminal cytosolic tail (amino acids 403–437).
evidence: This is stated as a fact with reference to UniProt database.

claim: The N-terminal lumenal domain of TGN46 comprises amino acids 22–381.
source: As TGN46 is a single-pass type-I TM protein of 437 amino acids (human TGN46, UniProt identifier O43493-2), we investigated whether functional cargo-packaging modules can be found in (1) the N-terminal lumenal domain (amino acids 22–381), (2) the single TM domain (TMD; amino acids 382–402), and/or (3) the short C-terminal cytosolic tail (amino acids 403–437).
evidence: This is stated as structural information about TGN46.

claim: The transmembrane domain of TGN46 comprises amino acids 382–402.
source: As TGN46 is a single-pass type-I TM protein of 437 amino acids (human TGN46, UniProt identifier O43493-2), we investigated whether functional cargo-packaging modules can be found in (1) the N-terminal lumenal domain (amino acids 22–381), (2) the single TM domain (TMD; amino acids 382–402), and/or (3) the short C-terminal cytosolic tail (amino acids 403–437).
evidence: This is stated as structural information about TGN46.

claim: The C-terminal cytosolic tail of TGN46 comprises amino acids 403–437.
source: As TGN46 is a single-pass type-I TM protein of 437 amino acids (human TGN46, UniProt identifier O43493-2), we investigated whether functional cargo-packaging modules can be found in (1) the N-terminal lumenal domain (amino acids 22–381), (2) the single TM domain (TMD; amino acids 382–402), and/or (3) the short C-terminal cytosolic tail (amino acids 403–437).
evidence: This is stated as structural information about TGN46.

claim: The cytosolic tail of TGN46 contains a tyrosine-based cytosolic motif (YQRL, amino acids 430–433).
source: This tail region contains a tyrosine-based cytosolic motif (YXXΦ; where X represents any amino acid, and Φ is an amino acid with bulky hydrophobic side chains Ohno et al., 1996; in TGN46: YQRL, amino acids 430–433).
evidence: This is stated as a structural feature with citation to prior work.

claim: The YQRL motif acts as an endocytic signal for plasma membrane internalization and trafficking back to the TGN.
source: This motif acts as an endocytic signal for PM internalization and trafficking back to the TGN, and is therefore crucial for the steady-state localization of TGN46 at TGN (Banting and Ponnambalam, 1997; Stanley and Howell, 1993; Rajasekaran et al., 1994; Bos et al., 1993; Humphrey et al., 1993; Banting et al., 1998).
evidence: This is stated as an established function with multiple citations.

claim: The YQRL motif is crucial for the steady-state localization of TGN46 at TGN.
source: This motif acts as an endocytic signal for PM internalization and trafficking back to the TGN, and is therefore crucial for the steady-state localization of TGN46 at TGN (Banting and Ponnambalam, 1997; Stanley and Howell, 1993; Rajasekaran et al., 1994; Bos et al., 1993; Humphrey et al., 1993; Banting et al., 1998).
evidence: This is stated as an established function with multiple citations.

claim: GFP-TGN46-∆cyt was partially present at the trans-Golgi membranes/TGN and partially at the plasma membrane.
source: As previously reported (Bos et al., 1993; Humphrey et al., 1993), GFP-TGN46-∆cyt was partially present at the trans-Golgi membranes/TGN and partially at the PM, as qualitatively seen in the micrographs (Figure 2).
evidence: This is stated as an observation consistent with prior literature, with reference to microscopy data.

claim: The trans-Golgi/TGN membranes are laterally compartmentalized into export domains (positive for TGN46) and processing domains (positive for sialyltransferase).
source: We and others have previously shown that the trans-Golgi/TGN membranes are laterally compartmentalized into export domains (positive for TGN46) and processing domains (positive for the late-Golgi glycosylation enzyme sialyltransferase, ST) (van Galen et al., 2014; Patterson et al., 2008; Tie et al., 2022).
evidence: This is stated as an established finding with citations to prior work.

claim: GFP-TGN46-∆cyt has a lower degree of intra-Golgi colocalization with TGN46-mRFP and a higher colocalization with ST-mCherry compared to GFP-TGN46 WT.
source: Our data show that GFP-TGN46-∆cyt has a lower degree of intra-Golgi colocalization with respect to TGN46-mRFP and a higher one with respect to ST-mCherry, as compared to its WT counterpart (Figure 2B, C).
evidence: The text states this observation with reference to quantitative colocalization data.

claim: GFP-TGN46-∆cyt shows an intra-Golgi localization pattern more closely resembling that of ST-GFP-positive processing domains.
source: Hence, GFP-TGN46-∆cyt shows an intra-Golgi localization pattern more closely resembling that of ST-GFP-positive processing domains (Figure 2B, C).
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the colocalization data.

claim: The cytosolic domain of TGN46 confers overall TGN localization by contributing to recycling from the plasma membrane and to fine steady-state partitioning into TGN export domains.
source: These data indicate that the cytosolic domain of TGN46 confers an overall TGN localization by contributing not only to the recycling from the PM, as previously reported (Bos et al., 1993; Humphrey et al., 1993), but also to its fine steady-state partitioning into TGN export domains and exclusion from processing domains.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the localization experiments, integrating new findings with prior literature.

claim: GFP-TGN46-∆cyt is preferentially exported in CARTS and not in VSVG carriers.
source: Our results indicated that GFP-TGN46-∆cyt is preferentially exported in CARTS and not in VSVG carriers, although this mutant cargo protein showed a modest but statistically significant reduction in its CARTS specificity as compared to GFP-TGN46 WT (Figure 2D, E).
evidence: The text states this observation with reference to carrier colocalization data.

claim: GFP-TGN46-∆cyt shows a modest but statistically significant reduction in CARTS specificity compared to GFP-TGN46 WT.
source: Our results indicated that GFP-TGN46-∆cyt is preferentially exported in CARTS and not in VSVG carriers, although this mutant cargo protein showed a modest but statistically significant reduction in its CARTS specificity as compared to GFP-TGN46 WT (Figure 2D, E).
evidence: The text states this observation with reference to quantitative data.

claim: GFP-TGN46-∆cyt exits the Golgi at a rate that is indistinguishable from that of GFP-TGN46 WT.
source: Interestingly, GFP-TGN46-∆cyt exits the Golgi at a rate that is indistinguishable from that of GFP-TGN46 WT (Figure 3A, B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The text states this observation with reference to FLIP experimental data.

claim: The cytosolic tail of TGN46 does not play a major role in mediating TGN46 incorporation into CARTS for export out of the TGN.
source: Taken together, our results suggest that, although the cytosolic tail of TGN46 is important for PM recycling, it does not play a major role in mediating TGN46 incorporation into CARTS for export out of the TGN.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the experiments on the cytosolic tail deletion mutant.

claim: The membrane thickness increases along the secretory pathway.
source: The membrane thickness increases along the secretory pathway (Mitra et al., 2004), which correlates with the average TMD length of the proteins of these organelles (Sharpe et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated as an established fact with citations.

claim: The average TMD length of proteins correlates with membrane thickness along the secretory pathway.
source: The membrane thickness increases along the secretory pathway (Mitra et al., 2004), which correlates with the average TMD length of the proteins of these organelles (Sharpe et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated as an established correlation with citation.

claim: TGN46 is a type-I protein with a single TMD of 21 amino acids.
source: TGN46 is a type-I protein with a single TMD of 21 amino acids, whereas ST (ST6Gal-I) is a type-II protein with a shorter TMD of 17 amino acids (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is stated as structural information with reference to a figure.

claim: ST (ST6Gal-I) is a type-II protein with a TMD of 17 amino acids.
source: TGN46 is a type-I protein with a single TMD of 21 amino acids, whereas ST (ST6Gal-I) is a type-II protein with a shorter TMD of 17 amino acids (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is stated as structural information with reference to a figure.

claim: Altering the TMD of TGN46 has no discernible impact on intra-Golgi localization.
source: First, we expressed different combinations of these proteins in HeLa cells, and monitored their intracellular localization by fluorescence microscopy. Altering the TMD of TGN46 had no discernible impact on intra-Golgi localization (Figure 4B, C), suggesting that the hydrophobic matching mechanism is not a major determinant for the fine intra-Golgi localization of TGN46.
evidence: The text states this observation with reference to microscopy data.

claim: The hydrophobic matching mechanism is not a major determinant for the fine intra-Golgi localization of TGN46.
source: First, we expressed different combinations of these proteins in HeLa cells, and monitored their intracellular localization by fluorescence microscopy. Altering the TMD of TGN46 had no discernible impact on intra-Golgi localization (Figure 4B, C), suggesting that the hydrophobic matching mechanism is not a major determinant for the fine intra-Golgi localization of TGN46.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the TMD alteration experiments.

claim: Even with super-resolution microscopy, the intra-Golgi localization of TGN46 mutants with shorter TMD was indistinguishable from that of TGN46 WT.
source: To address this possibility, we used super-resolution single-molecule localization microscopy with a localization precision (resolution) of ~15–30 nm. Our results show that, even with this enhanced spatial resolution, the intra-Golgi localization of the different TGN46 mutants with shorter TMD was indistinguishable from that of TGN46 WT (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The text states this observation from super-resolution microscopy experiments.

claim: The two mutants with shorter TMDs (TGN46-shortTMD and TGN46-ST TMD) lost their preference for being co-packaged with PAUF into CARTS.
source: Interestingly, the two mutants with shorter TMDs (TGN46-shortTMD and TGN46-ST TMD) lost their preference for being co-packaged with PAUF into CARTS, and partially redirected into other transport carriers such as VSVG carriers (Figure 4D, E), even though they keep a similar steady-state intra-Golgi localization as the TGN46 WT (Figure 4A).
evidence: The text states this observation with reference to carrier colocalization data.

claim: TGN46 mutants with shorter TMDs partially redirected into other transport carriers such as VSVG carriers.
source: Interestingly, the two mutants with shorter TMDs (TGN46-shortTMD and TGN46-ST TMD) lost their preference for being co-packaged with PAUF into CARTS, and partially redirected into other transport carriers such as VSVG carriers (Figure 4D, E), even though they keep a similar steady-state intra-Golgi localization as the TGN46 WT (Figure 4A).
evidence: The text states this observation with reference to carrier colocalization data.

claim: TGN46-ST TMD-GFP has a slower Golgi export rate (longer Golgi residence time) compared to TGN46-GFP.
source: FLIP experiments indicated that the chimeric protein TGN46-ST TMD-GFP has a slower Golgi export rate (longer Golgi residence time) as compared to TGN46-GFP.
evidence: The text states this observation from FLIP experiments.

claim: TGN46-shortTMD-GFP was exported at a slightly slower rate, although this difference was not statistically significant.
source: In addition, TGN46-shortTMD-GFP was exported at a slightly slower rate, although this difference was not statistically significant (Figure 3C, D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The text states this observation with reference to FLIP data.

claim: The Golgi residence time of TGN46-GFP was not affected by the co-expression of either TGN46-mRFP or TGN46-ST TMD-mRFP.
source: Our results show that the Golgi residence time of TGN46-GFP was not affected by the co-expression of either the WT or the chimeric proteins (Figure 4—figure supplement 3A, B).
evidence: The text states this observation from co-expression FLIP experiments.

claim: The slower Golgi export rate of TGN46 mutants with short TMDs is a consequence of their compromised selective sorting into CARTS without detectable changes in their intra-Golgi localization.
source: These data provide further support to the idea that the slower Golgi export rate of TGN46 mutants with short TMDs is a consequence of their compromised selective sorting into CARTS without detectable changes in their intra-Golgi localization.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the combined localization and export rate data.

claim: TGN46-GFP and TGN46-mRFP do not co-immunoprecipitate when expressed in HeLa cells.
source: To examine if the unaltered intra-Golgi localization of TGN46-shortTMD and TGN46-ST TMD compared to WT was due to protein dimerization/oligomerization, we tested whether TGN46-GFP and TGN46-mRFP co-immunoprecipitated when expressed in HeLa cells. Our results show no obvious dimerization between TGN46-GFP and TGN46-mRFP (Figure 4—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: The text states this observation from co-immunoprecipitation experiments.

claim: TGN46-∆cyt-ST TMD phenocopies GFP-TGN46-∆cyt regarding its intra-Golgi localization.
source: This chimeric protein phenocopies GFP-TGN46-∆cyt regarding its (1) intra-Golgi localization (Figure 2B, C and Figure 4B, C), and (2) CARTS specificity (Figure 2D, E and Figure 4D, E), with only a milder reduction in the Golgi export rate (Figure 3A, B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The text states this observation with reference to multiple figures.

claim: TGN46-∆cyt-ST TMD phenocopies GFP-TGN46-∆cyt regarding its CARTS specificity.
source: This chimeric protein phenocopies GFP-TGN46-∆cyt regarding its (1) intra-Golgi localization (Figure 2B, C and Figure 4B, C), and (2) CARTS specificity (Figure 2D, E and Figure 4D, E), with only a milder reduction in the Golgi export rate (Figure 3A, B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The text states this observation with reference to multiple figures.

claim: The hydrophobic matching mechanism does not play a primary role in driving the intra-Golgi localization and Golgi export of TGN46.
source: Taken together, these results strongly indicate that the hydrophobic matching mechanism (as well as the information encoded in the TMD) does not play a primary role in driving the intra-Golgi localization and Golgi export of TGN46.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the TMD manipulation experiments.

claim: GFP-TGN46-∆lum lost the characteristic intra-Golgi localization of TGN46 WT and rather localized into ST-mCherry-positive processing domains.
source: Although still perinuclear, GFP-TGN46-∆lum lost the characteristic intra-Golgi localization of the TGN46 WT and rather localized into ST-mCherry-positive processing domains of the trans-Golgi membranes (Figure 5B, C).
evidence: The text states this observation with reference to microscopy data.

claim: GFP-TGN46-∆lum shows a striking reduction in selective incorporation into CARTS compared to full-length TGN46.
source: Notably, this exclusion from TGN export domains paralleled a striking reduction in the selective incorporation of GFP-TGN46-∆lum into CARTS (Figure 6A, B), as well as in the rate of Golgi export (Figure 3F and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A, C), as compared to the full-length protein.
evidence: The text states this observation with reference to carrier colocalization data.

claim: GFP-TGN46-∆lum shows a reduction in the rate of Golgi export compared to full-length TGN46.
source: Notably, this exclusion from TGN export domains paralleled a striking reduction in the selective incorporation of GFP-TGN46-∆lum into CARTS (Figure 6A, B), as well as in the rate of Golgi export (Figure 3F and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A, C), as compared to the full-length protein.
evidence: The text states this observation with reference to FLIP data.

claim: The lumenal domain of TGN46 is necessary for CARTS-mediated export of TGN46.
source: These results consistently indicate that the lumenal domain of TGN46 is necessary for CARTS-mediated export of TGN46, therefore suggesting that this domain contains a signal for sorting and loading into CARTS.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the lumenal domain deletion experiments.

claim: The lumenal domain of TGN46 contains a signal for sorting and loading into CARTS.
source: These results consistently indicate that the lumenal domain of TGN46 is necessary for CARTS-mediated export of TGN46, therefore suggesting that this domain contains a signal for sorting and loading into CARTS.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the lumenal domain deletion experiments.

claim: GFP-TGN46lum maintained specificity for CARTS-mediated export.
source: Nonetheless, when we used our synchronized cargo release assay to measure selective incorporation into CARTS, GFP-TGN46lum maintained specificity for CARTS-mediated export (Figure 6A, B).
evidence: The text states this observation with reference to carrier colocalization data.

claim: GFP-TGN46lum exits as fast as GFP-TGN46 WT, or even faster.
source: Moreover, FLIP experiments revealed that GFP-TGN46lum exits as fast as GFP-TGN46 WT, or even faster (Figure 3E and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: The text states this observation with reference to FLIP data.

claim: GFP-ST-TGN46lum maintained a good degree of colocalization with ST-mCherry and additionally increased its colocalization with TGN46-mRFP.
source: Our results indicate that GFP-ST-TGN46lum maintained a good degree of colocalization with ST-mCherry and additionally it increased its colocalization with TGN46-mRFP (Figure 5B, C).
evidence: The text states this observation with reference to colocalization data.

claim: GFP-VSVG-TGN46lum specifically exits the TGN in CARTS, with a similar specificity to that of TGN46-GFP.
source: Despite these subtle differences in their intra-Golgi localization, the GFP-VSVG-TGN46lum chimera specifically exits the TGN in CARTS, with a similar specificity to that of TGN46-GFP, whereas GFP-VSVG-∆lum exits in VSVG carriers, similarly to VSVG-GFP (Figure 6A, B).
evidence: The text states this observation with reference to carrier colocalization data.

claim: GFP-VSVG-∆lum exits in VSVG carriers, similarly to VSVG-GFP.
source: Despite these subtle differences in their intra-Golgi localization, the GFP-VSVG-TGN46lum chimera specifically exits the TGN in CARTS, with a similar specificity to that of TGN46-GFP, whereas GFP-VSVG-∆lum exits in VSVG carriers, similarly to VSVG-GFP (Figure 6A, B).
evidence: The text states this observation with reference to carrier colocalization data.

claim: GFP-VSVG-TGN46lum has a fast Golgi export rate, indistinguishable from that of GFP-TGN46 WT.
source: In line with these observations, FLIP microscopy showed a fast Golgi export rate of GFP-VSVG-TGN46lum, indistinguishable from that of GFP-TGN46 WT, and a somewhat slower export rate for both GFP-VSVG-∆lum and VSVG-GFP (Figure 3F, G and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A, C, D).
evidence: The text states this observation with reference to FLIP data.

claim: GFP-VSVG-∆lum and VSVG-GFP have a somewhat slower Golgi export rate compared to GFP-VSVG-TGN46lum.
source: In line with these observations, FLIP microscopy showed a fast Golgi export rate of GFP-VSVG-TGN46lum, indistinguishable from that of GFP-TGN46 WT, and a somewhat slower export rate for both GFP-VSVG-∆lum and VSVG-GFP (Figure 3F, G and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A, C, D).
evidence: The text states this observation with reference to FLIP data.

claim: The lumenal domain of TGN46 can re-direct other TM cargo proteins into CARTS.
source: These results indicate that the lumenal domain of TGN46 can re-direct other TM cargo proteins into CARTS, thereby acting as a gain-of-function domain for fast export in CARTS out of the Golgi apparatus.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the chimeric protein experiments.

claim: The lumenal domain of TGN46 acts as a gain-of-function domain for fast export in CARTS out of the Golgi apparatus.
source: These results indicate that the lumenal domain of TGN46 can re-direct other TM cargo proteins into CARTS, thereby acting as a gain-of-function domain for fast export in CARTS out of the Golgi apparatus.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the chimeric protein experiments.

claim: GFP-ST-TGN46lum has a shorter Golgi residence time compared to ST-GFP.
source: Remarkably, GFP-ST-TGN46lum has a shorter Golgi residence time as compared to ST-GFP, with an export rate slightly slower but comparable to that of GFP-TGN46 WT (Figure 3F and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A, C).
evidence: The text states this observation with reference to FLIP data.

claim: Signals encoded in the lumenal domain of TGN46 are necessary and sufficient for cargo sorting into CARTS.
source: Altogether, these results indicate that, as long as the protein is correctly localized within the Golgi membranes, signals encoded in the lumenal domain of TGN46 are not only necessary, but also sufficient for cargo sorting into CARTS.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the lumenal domain experiments.

claim: There is a negative correlation between CARTS specificity and Golgi residence time (slope approximately −0.9 ± 0.4% min−1, r2 approximately 0.4).
source: The plots reveal the existence of a negative correlation between CARTS specificity and Golgi residence time (slope ~−0.9 ± 0.4% min−1, r2 ~ 0.4) (Figure 7A).
evidence: The text provides a specific quantitative correlation with reference to a plot.

claim: VSVG-containing carriers mediate a relatively slower Golgi export route compared to CARTS.
source: Taken together, these data indicate that VSVG-containing carriers mediate a relatively slower Golgi export route as compared to CARTS, thereby underscoring the different export kinetics of distinct Golgi export routes.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the correlation analysis.

claim: Overexpression of GFP-TGN46 WT or GFP-TGN46-∆cyt was able to rescue PAUF-mRFP export from the Golgi in TGN46-KO cells.
source: Interestingly, overexpression of GFP-TGN46 WT or GFP-TGN46-∆cyt – but not of TGN46-ST TMD-GFP or GFP-TGN46-∆lum – was able to rescue PAUF-mRFP export from the Golgi in TGN46-KO cells (Figure 7C, D and Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The text states this observation from rescue experiments with reference to FLIP data.

claim: Overexpression of TGN46-ST TMD-GFP or GFP-TGN46-∆lum was not able to rescue PAUF-mRFP export from the Golgi in TGN46-KO cells.
source: Interestingly, overexpression of GFP-TGN46 WT or GFP-TGN46-∆cyt – but not of TGN46-ST TMD-GFP or GFP-TGN46-∆lum – was able to rescue PAUF-mRFP export from the Golgi in TGN46-KO cells (Figure 7C, D and Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The text states this observation from rescue experiments with reference to FLIP data.

claim: The proper partitioning of TGN46 into TGN export domains is required for its lumenal domain to efficiently recruit and sort PAUF into nascent transport carriers for secretion.
source: Taken our data together, we propose a model in which the proper partitioning of TGN46 into TGN export domains (sites of CARTS biogenesis) is required for its lumenal domain to efficiently recruit and sort PAUF and possibly other CARTS cargoes into nascent transport carriers for secretion.
evidence: This is stated as a proposed model based on the experimental findings.

claim: TGN46 plays a novel role in the sorting of the secretory cargo protein PAUF into nascent transport carriers at the TGN.
source: Here, we revealed a novel role for TGN46 in the sorting of the secretory cargo protein PAUF into nascent transport carriers at the TGN.
evidence: This is stated as a summary of the main finding in the Discussion.

claim: TGN46 has been proposed to function as a secretory cargo receptor.
source: The single-pass type-I transmembrane (TM) protein TGN46 – or TGN38 in rodents (Ponnambalam et al., 1996) – has been proposed to function as a secretory cargo receptor (Stanley and Howell, 1993; Jones et al., 1993; Wang et al., 1995; Banting and Ponnambalam, 1997; McNamara et al., 2004; Wang and Howell, 2000; Ramazanov et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated as an established hypothesis with multiple citations.

claim: Direct evidence for a role of TGN46 in Golgi export has been lacking.
source: However, direct evidence for a role of TGN46 in Golgi export is lacking.
evidence: This is stated as a gap in the literature.

claim: TGN38 was first identified in rat cells and shown to have a well-defined steady-state localization at the TGN.
source: TGN38 was first identified in rat cells and shown to have a well-defined steady-state localization at the TGN (Luzio et al., 1990).
evidence: This is stated as an established fact with citation.

claim: TGN38 and its orthologs have become extensively employed as TGN marker proteins.
source: As a result, TGN38 and its orthologs have become extensively employed as TGN marker proteins.
evidence: This is stated as an established practice in the field.

claim: The amino acid sequence of rat TGN38 is largely conserved among other species, including humans (>80% amino acid identity between rat TGN38 and human TGN46).
source: The amino acid sequence of rat TGN38 is largely conserved among other species, including humans (>80% amino acid identity between rat TGN38 and human TGN46), with highly conserved cytosolic and TM domains and a somewhat less conserved lumenal domain (>60% overall identity but only ~25% in the bulk of the lumenal domain) (Ponnambalam et al., 1996).
evidence: This is stated as an established fact with citation.

claim: TGN38/TGN46 rapidly cycles between the TGN and the plasma membrane.
source: Despite having a steady-state TGN localization, TGN38/TGN46 rapidly cycles between the TGN and the plasma membrane (PM), exiting the TGN in specific carriers called CARTS (carriers of the TGN to the cell surface) (Wakana et al., 2012) and recycling from the PM back to the Golgi via early endosomes (Banting and Ponnambalam, 1997; Bos et al., 1993; Rajasekaran et al., 1994; Mallet and Maxfield, 1999; Humphrey et al., 1993).
evidence: This is stated as an established fact with multiple citations.

claim: CARTS were first identified by immuno-isolation of TGN46-containing transport carriers from the TGN to the PM.
source: CARTS were first identified by immuno-isolation of TGN46-containing transport carriers from the TGN to the PM (Wakana et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated as an established fact with citation.

claim: CARTS are formed in a protein kinase D (PKD)-dependent manner and contain the Rab6/Rab8 GTPases.
source: CARTS are formed in a protein kinase D (PKD)-dependent manner and contain the Rab6/Rab8 GTPases.
evidence: This is stated as an established characteristic of CARTS.

claim: CARTS traffic specific secretory cargoes, such as PAUF and lysozyme C, while excluding others, such as collagen I or VSVG.
source: CARTS traffic specific secretory cargoes, such as pancreatic adenocarcinoma upregulated factor (PAUF) and lysozyme C (LyzC), while exclude others, such as collagen I or vesicular stomatitis virus G-protein (VSVG) (Wakana et al., 2012; Wakana et al., 2013; Wakana and Campelo, 2021; Lujan et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated as an established characteristic of CARTS with citations.

claim: How secretory cargoes are sorted and specifically packed into CARTS is yet to be understood.
source: However, how secretory cargoes are sorted and specifically packed into CARTS is yet to be understood.
evidence: This is stated as a gap in knowledge.

claim: Whether TGN46 plays an active role in CARTS biogenesis or is just a passive TM cargo of this pathway is still unknown.
source: Furthermore, whether TGN46 plays an active role in CARTS biogenesis or it is just a passive TM cargo of this pathway is still unknown.
evidence: This is stated as a gap in knowledge that the study addresses.

claim: TGN46 is a heavily glycosylated protein, including nine predicted N-linked glycosylation sites, multiple O-linked glycosylation sites, and five phosphosites, all located at the lumenal domain.
source: On the one hand, TGN46 is a heavily glycosylated protein, including nine predicted N-linked glycosylation sites, multiple O-linked glycosylation sites, as well as five phosphosites (Figure 7—figure supplement 3B), all of them located at the lumenal domain.
evidence: This is stated as a structural feature with reference to a figure.

claim: The lumenal domain of TGN46 is highly disordered, as evidenced by a high PONDR score (in the range 0.5–1) for most of its amino acid sequence.
source: Structurally, this region is highly disordered, as evidenced by a high PONDR score (in the range 0.5–1) for most of its amino acid sequence (Figure 7—figure supplement 3C), indicating with high probability that the lumenal domain of TGN46 is an essentially intrinsically disordered region (IDR).
evidence: This is stated as an analysis result with reference to a figure.

claim: The lumenal domain of TGN46 is an essentially intrinsically disordered region (IDR).
source: Structurally, this region is highly disordered, as evidenced by a high PONDR score (in the range 0.5–1) for most of its amino acid sequence (Figure 7—figure supplement 3C), indicating with high probability that the lumenal domain of TGN46 is an essentially intrinsically disordered region (IDR).
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the PONDR analysis.

claim: The lumenal domain of TGN38 has been shown to interact with the adhesion receptor integrin β1.
source: Interestingly, the lumenal domain of TGN38 has been shown to interact with the adhesion receptor integrin β1 and to partially co-localize with integrins α5 and β1, but not αV or β3 (Wang and Howell, 2000).
evidence: This is stated as an established finding with citation.

claim: TGN38 regulates cell adhesion, as the overexpression of TGN38 leads to cell detachment from the substrate.
source: In addition, TGN38 regulates cell adhesion, as the overexpression of TGN38 leads to cell detachment from the substrate (Luzio et al., 1990; McNamara et al., 2004; Lee and Banting, 2002; Humphrey et al., 1993; Reaves et al., 1993).
evidence: This is stated as an established finding with multiple citations.

claim: Integrin β1 is transported from the TGN to the cell surface in a Rab6-mediated and PKD-dependent manner.
source: Remarkably, integrin β1 is transported from the TGN to the cell surface in a Rab6-mediated (Huet-Calderwood et al., 2017) and PKD-dependent manner (Yeaman et al., 2004).
evidence: This is stated as an established finding with citations.

claim: The role of TGN46 as a cargo receptor for the sorting of the soluble CARTS-specific cargo PAUF is quite general and can include a long list of both soluble and TM cargo proteins, such as α5β1 integrins.
source: Because CARTS are PKD-dependent transport carriers that share many similarities with Rab6-positive carriers (Wakana and Campelo, 2021), we propose that the role of TGN46 as a cargo receptor for the sorting of the soluble CARTS-specific cargo PAUF is quite general, and can include a long list of both soluble and TM cargo proteins, such as α5β1 integrins.
evidence: This is stated as a proposal based on the findings and prior literature.

claim: TGN46 binds a cytosolic protein complex made of 62 kDa protein (p62) and Rab6.
source: Interestingly, TGN46 binds a cytosolic protein complex made of 62 kDa protein (p62) and Rab6 (Jones et al., 1993).
evidence: This is stated as an established finding with citation.

claim: The budding of Golgi-derived carriers containing pIgA-R was blocked upon incubation of Golgi membranes with peptides against the cytosolic tail of TGN38/41.
source: These authors used a Golgi budding assay to test the involvement of the cytosolic domains of TGN38 and TGN41 in budding of Golgi-derived carriers that contain the TM cargo protein pIgA-R (polymeric IgA-receptor). The authors showed that the budding of these carriers was blocked upon incubation of the Golgi membranes with peptides against the cytosolic tail of TGN38/41.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from prior work with citation.

claim: TGN46 has been recently reported to assist in the trafficking of SARS-CoV-2.
source: In addition, TGN46 has been recently reported to assist in the trafficking of severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2), as this protein is upregulated in SARS-CoV-2-infected cells and cells depleted of TGN46 showed a reduced SARS-CoV-2 infection rate (Zhang et al., 2022).
evidence: This is stated as a recent finding with citation.

claim: TGN46 is upregulated in SARS-CoV-2-infected cells.
source: In addition, TGN46 has been recently reported to assist in the trafficking of severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2), as this protein is upregulated in SARS-CoV-2-infected cells and cells depleted of TGN46 showed a reduced SARS-CoV-2 infection rate (Zhang et al., 2022).
evidence: This is stated as a recent finding with citation.

claim: Cells depleted of TGN46 showed a reduced SARS-CoV-2 infection rate.
source: In addition, TGN46 has been recently reported to assist in the trafficking of severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2), as this protein is upregulated in SARS-CoV-2-infected cells and cells depleted of TGN46 showed a reduced SARS-CoV-2 infection rate (Zhang et al., 2022).
evidence: This is stated as a recent finding with citation.

claim: The levels of cholesterol and sphingomyelin are enriched along the cis- to trans-axis of the Golgi stack.
source: This mechanism builds on the observation that the levels of certain lipids, such as cholesterol and SM, are enriched along the cis- to trans-axis of the Golgi stack (van Meer et al., 2008; Bretscher and Munro, 1993).
evidence: This is stated as an established observation with citations.

claim: A comprehensive bioinformatic study showed a correlation between the intracellular localization of TM proteins and specific features of their TMDs, such as their length.
source: In addition, a comprehensive bioinformatic study using large datasets of TM proteins from different organisms showed a correlation between the intracellular localization of these proteins and different specific features of their TMDs, such as their length, which on average is shorter for proteins of the early secretory pathway as compared to those of the late secretory pathway (Sharpe et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated as an established finding with citation.

claim: The TMD length is on average shorter for proteins of the early secretory pathway compared to those of the late secretory pathway.
source: In addition, a comprehensive bioinformatic study using large datasets of TM proteins from different organisms showed a correlation between the intracellular localization of these proteins and different specific features of their TMDs, such as their length, which on average is shorter for proteins of the early secretory pathway as compared to those of the late secretory pathway (Sharpe et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated as an established finding with citation.

claim: Not only the TMD length but also the distribution of bulky and highly hydrophobic amino acids within the TMD affect the specific location of TM proteins.
source: Furthermore, it has been proposed that not only the TMD length but also the distribution of bulky and highly hydrophobic amino acids within the TMD affect the specific location of TM proteins (Sharpe et al., 2010; Quiroga et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated as a proposed mechanism with citations.

claim: Experimental data on the Golgi dynamics of secretory cargoes and Golgi residents cannot be explained if the hydrophobic matching mechanism is the sole retention mechanism for Golgi residents.
source: Interestingly, by using a coarse-grained mathematical model of intra-Golgi transport, Dmitrieff et al., 2013 showed that experimental data on the Golgi dynamics of secretory cargoes and Golgi residents cannot be explained if the hydrophobic matching mechanism is the sole retention mechanism for Golgi residents.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from a modeling study with citation.

claim: Hydrophobic mismatch between TMDs and bilayer thickness is not sufficient to drive the sorting of a TM Golgi-resident enzyme from substrate cargoes along the trans-Golgi/TGN membranes.
source: In agreement with this latter proposal, our results revealed that hydrophobic mismatch between TMDs and bilayer thickness is not sufficient to drive the sorting of a TM Golgi-resident enzymes from substrate cargoes along the trans-Golgi/TGN membranes.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the experimental results.

claim: Factors such as Vps74/GOLPH3 or coat proteins such as COPI influence enzyme–cargo interaction/segregation by recognizing cytoplasmic signals and thereby inducing protein retention by fast recycling.
source: Factors such as Vps74/GOLPH3 or coat proteins such as COPI (Tu et al., 2008; Wood et al., 2009; Welch et al., 2021), influence enzyme–cargo interaction/segregation by recognizing cytoplasmic signals and thereby inducing protein retention by fast recycling.
evidence: This is stated as an established mechanism with citations.

claim: Sphingomyelin metabolism can contribute to laterally organize the Golgi membranes at the nanoscale for efficient cargo–enzyme interactions.
source: In addition, SM metabolism can also contribute to laterally organize the Golgi membranes at the nanoscale for efficient cargo–enzyme interactions (Duran et al., 2012; van Galen et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated as an established mechanism with citations.

claim: CARTS appear to be a faster export route (approximately 15 min Golgi residence time) than VSVG carriers (approximately 30 min Golgi residence time).
source: In particular, when we compared the export rate of two different PKD-dependent TM proteins (TGN46, which is exported in CARTS; and VSVG, which is not), we found that CARTS appear to be a faster export route (~15 min Golgi residence time) than VSVG carriers (~30 min Golgi residence time) (Figure 7A).
evidence: The text provides specific quantitative measurements with reference to a figure.

claim: Loss of CARTS specificity correlated with larger Golgi residence times.
source: Remarkably, when we generated a series of chimeras combining different domains from different proteins, we observed that loss of CARTS specificity correlated with larger Golgi residence times (Figure 7A).
evidence: The text states this observation with reference to a figure.

claim: CARTS have been suggested to be enriched in cholesterol and sphingomyelin.
source: CARTS have been suggested to be enriched in cholesterol and SM (Wakana et al., 2021; Wakana and Campelo, 2021), and their biogenesis to require intact ER–Golgi membrane contact sites (MCS) supplying the TGN with these lipids (or their precursors) (Wakana et al., 2015; Wakana et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated as a suggested characteristic with citations.

claim: CARTS biogenesis requires intact ER–Golgi membrane contact sites supplying the TGN with cholesterol and sphingomyelin (or their precursors).
source: CARTS have been suggested to be enriched in cholesterol and SM (Wakana et al., 2021; Wakana and Campelo, 2021), and their biogenesis to require intact ER–Golgi membrane contact sites (MCS) supplying the TGN with these lipids (or their precursors) (Wakana et al., 2015; Wakana et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated as a suggested requirement with citations.

claim: TGN46 is a native cargo of the sphingomyelin-dependent TGN export pathway.
source: Notably, data from Deng, Pakdel et al. suggested that TGN46 is a native cargo of the SM-dependent TGN export pathway, as it was identified by mass spectrometry to be co-packaged in carriers containing the lumenal SM sensor EQ-SM-APEX2 (Deng et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated as a suggested finding with citation.

claim: TGN46 could be enriched in ER–Golgi membrane contact sites.
source: Given the similarities between the SM/Cab45 and CARTS export pathways (Stalder and Gershlick, 2020; Wakana and Campelo, 2021), it is tempting to speculate that TGN46 could be enriched in ER–Golgi MCS and perhaps complement the sorting function of Cab45 for a subset of secretory cargo proteins.
evidence: This is stated as speculation based on pathway similarities.

claim: TGN46 could complement the sorting function of Cab45 for a subset of secretory cargo proteins.
source: Given the similarities between the SM/Cab45 and CARTS export pathways (Stalder and Gershlick, 2020; Wakana and Campelo, 2021), it is tempting to speculate that TGN46 could be enriched in ER–Golgi MCS and perhaps complement the sorting function of Cab45 for a subset of secretory cargo proteins.
evidence: This is stated as speculation based on pathway similarities.
